rejected.title: Motor units
card: A motor unit is one motor neuron (nerve cell) and all the muscle fibres it controls. A muscle contains many motor units.
When the neuron sends a signal, every fibre in its unit contracts fully, or none of them contracts. This is the all-or-none principle.
Small motor units are recruited first. They have fewer fibres and make small, fine movements. Larger units join in when more force is needed.
A muscle makes more force by recruiting more and larger motor units. Signalling each unit more often, called frequency of stimulation, also adds force.
rejected.remember: One neuron plus its fibres is a motor unit. More force comes from recruiting more, larger units, small ones first.

a.q: Which describes the all-or-none principle for a single motor unit?
opts: All its fibres contract fully, or none do
Its fibres contract partly when little force is needed
Only some of its fibres contract at low effort
Its fibres contract in turn, one at a time
a.why: When the neuron sends a signal, every fibre in that unit contracts fully. A unit cannot give a partial contraction, so low effort does not mean some fibres or weaker fibres. The muscle uses fewer units instead.
a.clue: A single unit has no setting between off and fully on.

b.q: Sam picks up a pen, then lifts a heavy box of books. How does his muscle change its force for the box?
opts: It recruits more and larger motor units
Its active fibres switch to partial contractions
It switches off its small motor units
It recruits large units before the small ones
b.why: The box needs more force, so larger units join the small ones already working. The small units stay on, because they are recruited first, not swapped out. Fibres never give partial contractions under the all-or-none principle.
b.clue: Think about which units join in, and in what order.

draft.title: Motor units
card: A motor unit is one motor neuron (nerve cell) and all the muscle fibres it controls. A muscle contains many motor units.
When the neuron sends a signal, every fibre in its unit contracts fully, or none of them contracts. This is the all-or-none principle.

draft.remember: One nerve plus its fibres is a unit, and a muscle gets stronger by recruiting more units.

a.q: Which describes the all-or-none principle for a single motor unit?
opts: All its fibres contract fully, or none do
Its fibres contract more strongly for harder tasks
Only some of its fibres contract at low effort
Its fibres contract in turn, one at a time
a.why: When the neuron fires, every fibre in that unit contracts fully. A unit cannot give a partial contraction. Force changes by recruiting more units, not by each unit contracting harder.
a.clue: A single unit has no setting between off and fully on.

b.q: Sam picks up a pen, then lifts a heavy box of books. How does his muscle change its force for the box?
opts: It recruits more and larger motor units
Each active motor unit contracts harder
It switches off its small motor units
It recruits only one very large motor unit
b.why: More force needs more motor units, and larger ones join the small ones already working. A single unit cannot contract harder than fully. The small units are not switched off.
b.clue: Units cannot vary their strength, so what can change?

b.best: It recruits more and larger motor units

problems.detail: The card says a muscle makes a stronger contraction by recruiting more units, 'not by making each unit contract harder'. This is too absolute. Force also rises with the frequency of stimulation (rate coding, or summation): a unit fired more often produces more tension. VCE resources commonly list frequency of stimulation as a factor in muscle force. The all-or-none principle covers a single impulse, not the unit's total force output.

The clue 'Units cannot vary their strength' and the why 'A single unit cannot contract harder than fully' rule out rate coding. Under that mechanism, 'Each active motor unit contracts harder' is partly true, because faster firing increases each unit's force. Keep the intended answer, but soften the clue and the why, for example 'the main way is recruiting more units'.
'A muscle gets stronger' can be read as long-term strength gains from training, not the force of a single contraction. Say 'makes more force' instead.

check.summary: Both questions have a single right answer. However, the card, the clue for (b) and the why for (b) state absolutely that a unit's force cannot vary, which ignores frequency of stimulation (rate coding), a recognised factor in VCE. The remember line's 'gets stronger' is also ambiguous.
